A hedge fund charges incentive fees subject to certain constraints that include the following:
The hurdle rate, which is the minimum total return, either net or gross of management fees, that the fund must earn before it receives an incentive fee. The hurdle rate can be either:
soft, so that the incentive fee is based on the entire profit, or
hard, so that the incentive fee is based on only returns in excess of the hurdle rate.
The high-water mark, a base asset value used to calculate the incentive fee. It is the fund's previous peak value of assets under management that resulted in an incentive fee.
In this scenario, the fund's net performance (ie, after management fees) of 30% cleared all the given hurdle rates, which entitles the fund to an incentive fee. The soft hurdle rate allows the fund to collect the incentive fee on the entire gain above the high-water mark (ie, 10% of $30 million = $3 million).
(Choice B) This structure implies a $3.6 million incentive fee (ie, 12% of $30 million). However, the incentive fee in this scenario is $3 million. The soft hurdle rate of 10% allows the fund to collect on the entire gain above the high-water mark of $100 million (ie, 130 − 100 = 30).
(Choice C) Given a high-water mark of $100 million and a 10% hard hurdle rate, the fund would receive an incentive fee on only the gains above the hurdle rate. The fund's net performance of 30% minus 10% equals 20%, and 20% of $100 million is $20 million, so the incentive fee would be 10% of $20 million (ie, $2 million).

An investor's return is calculated net of fees and as a percentage of the fund's beginning value. Hedge funds often levy both a management fee and an incentive fee.
The management fee is calculated as a percentage of the fund's total ending assets under management (AUM) and is assessed regardless of profitability.
The incentive fee is calculated as a percentage of profits either net (ie, after deducting) or gross (ie, before deducting) of management fees.
If fees are calculated independently, the hurdle rate determination and fee calculations are on a gross basis.
An incentive fee is often contingent on profits being greater than a hurdle rate and/or AUM being higher than the high-water mark. In this scenario, the fund's threshold to earn an incentive fee is contingent on exceeding the 5% soft hurdle rate and the high-water mark of $380 million. Due to the soft hurdle rate, the incentive fee will be applied to the entire gain above the high-water mark.
The investor's return for the year is calculated (in $ millions) as follows:

| Steps | Calculations | |
|---|---|---|
| Calculate profit before fees | Ending AUM | 412 |
| | Beginning AUM | (372) |
| | Profit before fees | 40 |
| Hurdle rate determination* | (40 ÷ 372) | 10.75% |
| Calculate management fee | Management fee (412 × 0.015) | (6.18) |
| Calculate incentive fee | Profit before fees | 40 |
| | High-water mark adjustment (380 − 372) | (8) |
| | Incentive fee base | 32 |
| | Incentive fee (32 × 0.12) | (3.84) |
| Calculate investor return | Profit before fees | 40 |
| | Management fee | (6.18) |
| | Incentive fee | (3.84) |
| | Profit after fees | 29.98 |
| | Investor return (29.98 ÷ 372) | 8.06% |

*Incentive fee earned as 10.75% > 5% hurdle rate and ending AUM of 412 > the HWM of 380

(Choice A) A 7.80% return inappropriately calculates returns using beginning AUM, instead of the high-water mark, as the incentive fee's base.
(Choice C) An 8.67% return inappropriately calculates returns using a hard hurdle rate.

"Members and Candidates must not engage in practices that distort prices or artificially inflate trading volume with the intent to mislead market participants."
Standard II(B) Market Manipulation prohibits activities by Members or Candidates that deceive market participants by distorting securities prices or volumes. Manipulation can occur through: information-based activities (eg, issuing false or misleading information) and/or transaction-based activities (eg, exaggerated trading between two accounts).
The Standard does not prevent the use of legitimate trading strategies, even if they cause price movements or are designed to purposefully limit the impact on the market. The key element in determining whether the Standard is violated is intent: if the strategy is intended to deceive investors, it violates the Standard.
In this scenario, if Zhao Fen traded Formula Industries stock between her personal accounts, it would give market participants a false impression of higher trading volume since the trading is not done between unique market participants. Deceiving participants through transaction-based manipulation violates the Standard.
(Choice A) Using an intermediary (eg, block house) to sell the position outside the market or break the order into smaller batches is a legitimate trading strategy. This practice aims to reduce a sale's impact on the market, but the resulting trades are done with other market participants and therefore do not violate the Standard.
(Choice B) While selling all the holdings in one position might drive down the price, Zhao may do so without intending to manipulate market participants; therefore, it is not the action most likely to violate the Standard. The Standards do not require Members or Candidates to disadvantage themselves to uphold market integrity, so this strategy can be used if cash is needed quickly.

"Members and Candidates have a duty of loyalty to their clients and must act with reasonable care and exercise prudent judgment. Members and Candidates must act for the benefit of their clients and place their clients' interests before their employer's or their own interests."
Standard III(A) Loyalty, Prudence, and Care requires Members and Candidates to seek best price and best execution for client trades. "Best price" and "best execution" do not necessarily mean the lowest trading commission, but commissions paid to brokers to execute the trades must be commensurate with the value received.
Soft dollar brokerage refers to the practice of using a portion of brokerage commissions to purchase investment services (eg, research). Since the client "pays" the commission out of client assets, these investment services are the property of the client, not the investment management firm, and must be used to benefit the client. Typically, brokers that offer value-added investment services charge higher commissions. Clients can choose not to have their accounts traded on a soft dollar basis if they do not feel the value is worth the cost.
In this scenario, Johnson does not violate the Standard even though he directs all account trading to RMB. RMB reduced its commissions to match CCB's commissions; therefore, the clients that do not allow soft dollars are not paying extra to subsidize the research used by clients that allow soft dollars (Choice C). "Members and Candidates who possess material nonpublic information that could affect the value of an investment must not act or cause others to act on the information."
Standard II(A) Material Nonpublic Information prohibits members and candidates from trading on material nonpublic information. "Material" refers to information that would be expected to cause a significant change in the market price of a security. "Nonpublic" means that the information has not been disseminated to the general investing marketplace. Information that is given only to a limited group of investors, such as to analysts on a conference call, does not make that information public.
The Standard also prohibits members and candidates from recommending investments to others if the recommendation is based on material nonpublic information. It is irrelevant whether the recipient acts on the recommendation.
Pressly violated the Standard both by purchasing the stock and advising her father to buy it. The CEO's information is clearly material since the expected boost to Prime Health's revenues from regulatory approval of the drug will likely affect PrimeHealth's stock price. The information was also nonpublic since only a few analysts knew it when Pressly bought the stock.
